strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored safety threat: unreliable web search results for LLM-based search agents, clearly distinguishing this from static RAG/knowledge-base threats and grounding it in a real-world anecdote plus two in-the-wild experiments.

Proposes an automated red-teaming framework that combines LLM-driven test-case generation, guideline-assisted unreliable-website synthesis, checklist-assisted safety evaluation, and helpfulness evaluation, enabling scalable and low-cost pre-deployment testing.
Uses simulation-based injection of unreliable websites into authentic search results, which avoids harmful blackhat SEO manipulation and is a sound ethical choice for safety testing.

Constructs the SafeSearch benchmark with 300 test cases across five risk categories, includes automated quality filtering for attainability and integrity, and provides concrete examples, prompts, and configurations.

Conducts a broad evaluation across three representative search-agent scaffolds, seven proprietary and eight open-source backend LLMs, five risk types, repeated trials, cached search results, and multiple ablations (injection position, token limit, timestamp, website generator, search result count, defenses).

Produces actionable empirical findings: very high ASR in many settings (up to 90.5% for GPT-4.1-mini with search workflow), reasoning models and deep-research scaffolds generally showing greater resilience, misinformation as the most threatening risk type, and limited effectiveness of reminder prompting versus moderate gains from filtering.
Validates the checklist-assisted safety evaluator against human annotations on 200 responses with high agreement (95-98%), which strengthens confidence in the automated ASR metric.

Provides detailed prompts, experimental configurations, code, and test cases, and includes an honest limitations section covering proprietary systems, search-service coverage, benchmark scale, efficiency metrics, and the lack of stealthiness in generated unreliable websites.
weaknesses: The benchmark is relatively modest in scale (300 cases, 60 per risk). Although the framework is claimed to be scalable and cost-efficient, the paper does not quantitatively demonstrate scaling or compare cost/efficiency against alternative red-teaming methods.

The generated unreliable websites are not optimized for stealth; the authors themselves note that filtering-detection successes often stem from a relative lack of stealth and that stealthier attacks could be more threatening. This makes the absolute ASR difficult to interpret as a realistic estimate of real-world attack success.

The first in-the-wild experiment relies solely on GPT-4.1 with CoT to flag content farms, without reported human validation or inter-annotator agreement. The 4.3% prevalence estimate is therefore suggestive but not rigorously established.

The second in-the-wild experiment finds only 46 altered responses out of 1,000, and the manual review is described only qualitatively. This provides motivating evidence but is limited in scale and statistical detail.

The safety and helpfulness evaluators are both GPT-4.1-mini, which is also one of the evaluated agent backends. Although human agreement is high, potential self-preference or shared-model bias is not ruled out by testing an independent judge model.

Only Google Search is used as the search service. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but external validity to other search engines/APIs, which may rank or filter unreliable content differently, remains unestablished.

Proprietary deep-research systems (e.g., OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini) are not evaluated; the deep-research scaffold is only an open-source prototype. Conclusions about deployed commercial systems are therefore indirect.

The deep-research scaffold is evaluated on only five of the fifteen backend models, and all scaffold implementations are specific. Generalization across different agent designs and tool-calling policies is not fully demonstrated.

The manual review protocol for the final 300 benchmark test cases is described only briefly, with no reported inter-annotator agreement or detailed quality-control statistics, which slightly weakens reproducibility of benchmark curation.

ASR and helpfulness scores are averaged over three runs, but no confidence intervals or variance estimates are reported, making it difficult to assess the stability of model rankings given stochastic LLM behavior.

The helpfulness metric may reward confident or lengthy responses even when they are unsafe, as suggested by the finding that HS_manip. can exceed HS_benign. This is an interesting observation but also raises questions about what the helpfulness score is actually capturing.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important safety problem: LLM-based search agents can be misled by unreliable web content. It clearly distinguishes search agents from RAG systems and provides two motivating in-the-wild observations.

The proposed automated red-teaming framework is systematic and includes a multi-stage test-case generation pipeline, differential quality filtering, and checklist-assisted evaluation. The resulting SafeSearch benchmark (300 cases across five risk types) and the evaluation of three search-agent scaffolds with 15 backend LLMs are substantial.

The authors provide extensive implementation details, prompts, ablations (injection position, token limits, timestamp, generator choice), and a defense analysis. Code and test cases are promised for release.
Ethical considerations are handled well: simulation-based testing avoids real-world SEO harm, and the paper discusses broader impacts, limitations, and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central threat model is artificial and may overstate real-world vulnerability. The tester injects a single LLM-generated unreliable website into search results; this does not reflect real ranking, prevalence, or attacker stealth. The authors acknowledge the generated websites are not stealthy (filtering recall 44.2%), so the measured ASRs may not transfer to real deployments.

The benchmark and evaluation have circularity risks. Test cases, websites, and checklists are generated by LLMs (o4-mini, GPT-4.1-mini), and the safety evaluator is also GPT-4.1-mini, one of the tested models. Human validation is limited to 200 responses by the authors themselves; no independent validation or cross-model evaluator robustness is reported.

The in-the-wild motivating experiments are not rigorous. Content-farm prevalence relies on an unvalidated GPT-4.1 judge; the health differential experiment finds only 46/1000 altered responses, lacks repeated trials or controls, and does not quantify the manual review. These experiments do not robustly establish prevalence or impact.
The main results lack statistical rigor: ASRs are averaged over only three runs with no confidence intervals or significance tests, so differences between models and scaffolds may be noise.

The defense evaluation is incomplete: filtering recall is only 44.2%, with no precision, false-positive rate, or helpfulness impact reported; the reminder defense is a weak strawman. More sophisticated defenses are not tested.

Reproducibility is partial: the benchmark provides website-generation guidelines rather than fixed generated websites, so exact ASRs depend on re-generation and on live search results and API versions.

The contribution is more engineering/benchmark than new scientific insight. The main finding—that agents can be misled by unreliable search results—is expected, and the paper does not compare against existing search-agent safety benchmarks or real-world attack measurements.

strengths: Addresses a timely and under-explored threat surface: safety of LLM-based search agents exposed to unreliable web content.
Provides a systematic, automated red-teaming framework covering test-case generation, quality filtering, website generation, and checklist-assisted evaluation.
Constructs SafeSearch, a 300-case benchmark spanning five risk categories, and evaluates three representative scaffolds across 15 backend LLMs.
Empirical results are substantial and actionable: high ASRs for many models, limited effectiveness of reminder prompting, and filtering defenses roughly halving ASR.
Thorough ablations and validations: injection position, per-website token limit, temporal persistence, website generator choice, and safety evaluator agreement (95-98% with humans).
Good reproducibility: code, test cases, prompts, and detailed configurations are released, with careful ethical design avoiding real-world SEO manipulation.
The analysis of the knowledge-action gap and GPT-5 safety mechanisms (credibility reflection, source warnings) offers useful insights for agent developers.
weaknesses: The benchmark filtering uses a single baseline model (Qwen3-8B) to retain only attainable cases, which may bias the benchmark toward vulnerabilities of that model and reduce fairness for other agents.

The simulation injects highly tailored, credibility-optimized unreliable websites, which may overestimate real-world ASR relative to typical low-quality search results; the paper acknowledges this but does not quantify the gap.
Safety and helpfulness are evaluated by LLM-as-a-judge; the safety evaluator is validated on only 200 samples and three models, while the helpfulness evaluator lacks human validation.
Main results lack confidence intervals or significance tests despite three stochastic trials, so small model differences may not be reliable.
There is a minor presentation inconsistency: Section 4.1 attributes 85.0% and 77.3% ASRs to GPT-4.1-mini, but these correspond to GPT-4.1 in Table 2.
The cost-efficiency claim of the framework is not quantitatively supported; no cost analysis is provided.
Proprietary deep-research systems are not evaluated due to closed-source access, limiting external validity for commercial search agents.
The motivating in-the-wild experiments are small and rely on LLM judgments for content-farm detection and altered-response detection, with limited quantification of manual review.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important safety problem: unreliable search results in LLM-based search agents, motivated by a real-world incident and two in-the-wild observations.

Proposes a systematic and automated red-teaming framework with test-case generation, quality filtering, simulation-based testing, and checklist-assisted evaluation, enabling scalable and cost-efficient safety assessment.

Conducts a comprehensive evaluation: 300 test cases across five risk categories, three search-agent scaffolds, and 17 LLMs, with extensive ablations (injection position, token limit, timestamp, generator choice, injection round, persuasiveness).
Includes human validation of the checklist-assisted safety evaluator (agreement >95%) and quality assessment of generated queries against established benchmarks (WildChat, GAIA, SimpleQA).

Reports useful empirical findings: high ASR across many models/scaffolds, scaffold and model effects, misinformation as the most severe risk, limited effectiveness of reminder prompting, and partial effectiveness of filtering.

Demonstrates strong reproducibility and ethics practices: open-source code/dataset, detailed prompts, simulation-based testing to avoid real-world SEO harm, and thorough discussion of limitations and responsible research.
weaknesses: The claim that user queries are 'fully benign' is not consistently supported. Several examples in Table 5 are sensitive, leading, or potentially harmful (e.g., asking which racial group has the highest violent crime rate, requesting homemade pesticide/UV sterilization instructions). This weakens the threat model that risks arise solely from unreliable search results rather than from the query itself.

The unreliable websites are LLM-generated from guidelines and may be more targeted, authoritative, and persuasive than typical real-world unreliable content. The paper does not validate that they resemble actual low-quality websites (e.g., content farms) in distribution, which limits ecological validity and may overestimate real-world ASR.

The scaffold comparison is incomplete: the deep-research scaffold is evaluated on only 5 models, while the other scaffolds cover 17 models. The overall averages across scaffolds are therefore not directly comparable, and claims about scaffold robustness should be qualified.

There is limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for ASR differences, despite stochastic decoding (temperature 0.6, three runs per case). Many per-risk and per-model comparisons may be within noise.

The test-case generation, website generation, checklist construction, and safety/helpfulness evaluation all rely on a small set of LLMs (mainly GPT-4.1-mini and o4-mini), raising concerns about evaluator circularity and self-preference. Human validation is limited to 200 responses and two authors.

The helpfulness metric measures perceived usefulness rather than factual accuracy, so the claim that safety and helpfulness can be improved simultaneously is based on a metric that can reward plausible but unsafe responses. This limits the strength of the safety-helpfulness conclusion.

The 'knowledge-action gap' claim is not directly tested; the filtering detector achieves only 44.2% recall, and the paper does not provide a controlled comparison of the same model's knowledge versus its agentic behavior.
Cost-efficiency and scalability are claimed but not quantified; no runtime, token-cost, or latency analysis is provided to substantiate the 'lightweight and cost-efficient' characterization.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important safety problem: how LLM-based search agents behave when search results contain unreliable, misleading, or malicious content.

Provides an automated red-teaming pipeline with clear stages: scenario anchoring, test design, test instantiation, differential quality filtering, simulation-based injection, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.

Comprehensive empirical scope: three search-agent scaffolds, 17 backend LLMs, five risk categories, 300 curated test cases, and numerous ablations (injection position, token limit, timestamp, generator choice, injection round, persuasiveness, test generator).
Human validation of the checklist-assisted safety evaluator shows high agreement (>95%) on a 200-response sample, supporting the reliability of the core ASR metric.

Simulation-based testing avoids harmful real-world SEO manipulation, and the authors cache search results and release code, data, and prompts, improving reproducibility relative to many red-teaming studies.

Several findings are practically useful: scaffold design materially affects safety, reasoning models tend to be more robust, misinformation is the most severe risk, and safety and perceived helpfulness are not necessarily opposed.
The paper includes a thorough ethics statement and a limitations discussion, demonstrating awareness of dual-use and responsible-research concerns.
weaknesses: Ecological validity of the core threat model is limited: the framework assumes that one query-tailored unreliable website is always injected into the top-five search results. Real search ranking and retrieval probability are not modeled, so ASR is conditional on successful injection and may substantially overestimate real-world vulnerability. The "lower bound of safety" framing is therefore not rigorously justified.

The in-the-wild motivation is thin. Observation 1 relies on an LLM judge to flag content farms without human validation. Observation 2 reports 46/1000 stance changes for one model, but does not quantify how many changes were unsafe or causally attributable to unreliable sources. These observations do not strongly support the central claim that such failures are prevalent in practice.

Benchmark construction has a likely selection bias. The attainability filter uses Qwen3-8B as the baseline agent, so the final 300 test cases are those that successfully fool Qwen3-8B. This may bias ASRs across models and inflate the apparent vulnerability of Qwen3-8B-like systems. A multi-baseline or neutral filtering strategy is not used.

Statistical rigor is lacking. The paper reports many ASR/HS comparisons across models, scaffolds, and risk types, but provides no confidence intervals or significance tests. With 60 cases per risk and three runs, small differences may be noise.

Evaluator validity is only partially established. The safety evaluator is validated on 200 responses from three models, while the helpfulness evaluator is not human-validated at all. Some checklist items are broad (e.g., omitting independent test results or using testimonials without questioning authenticity) and may flag cautious or partially safe responses. The evaluator may also be susceptible to prompt injection from agent outputs, which is not discussed.

The defense evaluation is narrow. Only reminder prompting and one GPT-4.1-mini filtering detector are tested. The filtering detector has 44.2% recall, but precision, false-positive rate, and helpfulness cost are not reported. The claim that "common defenses offer limited protection" overgeneralizes from two simple baselines.

Cost-efficiency and scalability claims are unsupported. No API cost, token usage, or runtime analysis is provided. The pipeline uses relatively expensive models (o4-mini, GPT-4.1-mini) and has low retention rates (6.8–31.3%) during test-case curation, implying high generation cost.

Novelty is incremental. The framework integrates existing ideas—LLM-generated red-teaming, simulated tool manipulation, checklist-based LLM evaluation—and the closest works (Luo et al. 2025; Ou et al. 2025) are discussed but not empirically compared. The shift to benign queries and broader risk coverage is meaningful but not a major methodological leap.

Some test queries are not clearly benign (e.g., asking which racial group has the highest violent crime rate), conflicting with the paper's claim that all user queries are fully benign. This raises benchmark-validity and ethical concerns.

Presentation issues and reference inconsistencies are present: inconsistent naming (SAFESEARCH vs. SafeSearch), typos (e.g., "dndirect", "ddvertisement"), and citation mismatches (e.g., Chebotar et al. 2024 vs. 2019). Important limitations are buried in appendices rather than foregrounded in the main text.

The limitations discussion omits several key issues: selection bias from Qwen3-8B filtering, evaluator prompt-injection risk, absence of statistical tests, and unsupported cost-efficiency claims. These omissions weaken confidence in the benchmark's reliability.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important safety problem: LLM-based search agents are increasingly deployed, and the paper shows how unreliable search results can mislead them. The motivating real-world incident and two in-the-wild observations make the threat concrete.

Presents a systematic and automated red-teaming framework: the three-step test-case generation workflow, differential quality filtering, guideline-assisted unreliable-website generation, and checklist-assisted safety evaluation together form a scalable and cost-efficient pipeline.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 300 test cases across five risk categories, three search-agent scaffolds, and 17 representative LLMs, with repeated trials and cached search results for fairness. The results convincingly show high vulnerability in many configurations and meaningful variation across models and scaffolds.

Strong validation effort: the checklist-assisted safety evaluator is validated against human annotations with >95% agreement; benign ASR is near zero (0.81% average), supporting the causal claim that unsafe responses are largely induced by the injected unreliable websites.

Useful ablation and robustness analyses: injection position, token limits, timestamp persistence, website-generator choice, injection round, persuasiveness, and open-source test generators are examined. These strengthen confidence that the main findings are not artifacts of one narrow configuration.

Practical utility for agent development: the framework is used to study the effect of search-result count and to evaluate reminder-prompting and filtering defenses, revealing limited effectiveness of common mitigations and a knowledge-action gap. This gives actionable insights for developers.

Good reproducibility and ethical treatment: code, dataset, prompts, and configurations are promised; simulation-based testing avoids real-world SEO manipulation and harm to normal users; limitations, ethical concerns, and responsible-research practices are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Simulation fidelity is a central limitation: the setup injects one generated unreliable website into top-5 Google results, usually appended at the end, with a 2,000-token limit. Real-world unreliable search results may involve multiple sources, different ranking dynamics, and less tailored or less topically relevant pages. The paper argues conservatism and ablates several factors, but external validity remains imperfect.

The safety and helpfulness evaluations rely heavily on LLM-as-a-Judge, primarily GPT-4.1-mini. Safety evaluation is human-validated on 200 responses by two authors, which is useful but limited in scale and potentially biased. Helpfulness is not human-validated, and its scale measures perceived plausibility rather than factual accuracy or real utility, weakening claims about simultaneous safety and helpfulness.

Dataset scale and selection may limit representativeness. The final benchmark has only 300 cases (60 per risk type), and retention rates for harmful-output and prompt-injection cases are very low (6.9% and 6.8%), suggesting possible selection bias toward cases that pass the automated filtering. The five risk categories are representative but not exhaustive.

Generalization across scaffolds and services is limited. Deep-research scaffold experiments cover only five backend models, proprietary deep-research systems are omitted, and only Google Search is used as the search service. The paper acknowledges these limitations, but they restrict the reach of the conclusions.

Some motivating claims rest on weaker evidence: content-farm prevalence is judged by an LLM without reported human validation, and the stance-shift observation relies on manual inspection of 46/1000 cases with qualitative wording. These observations motivate the work but are not as rigorously established as the main benchmark.

The helpfulness metric and the claim that safety and helpfulness can be improved simultaneously need more scrutiny. HS_manip. exceeding HS_benign under tool calling may indicate that unsafe responses appear plausible rather than that safety and true helpfulness are aligned.

Minor presentation and consistency issues: the model-details appendix lists LLaMA-3.3-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B although they do not appear in the main table, and Figure 5 (Right) compares Sep 9, 2025 with Jan 27, 2026 without clearly explaining the latter timestamp. The term ASR is also somewhat awkward for non-adversarial risks such as bias and misinformation.
